title: Hotel bands, territory bands and how bands rose
summary: Whiteman and Lopez at Saratoga, territory bands, the Les Brown origin and shifting personnel.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money

blocks.x: Vincent Lopez. Uh, he's still going, you know. He ought to write a book, that guy, because he's been around an awful lot of music for an awful long time. Vincent Lopez.
I had some early jazz musicians, when I forget who there were, too.

I had some, there weren't, in the early 1920s, there weren't so many big bands, but what all of them would have some jazz musicians. I wouldn't imagine that if Whiteman had come along in the 30s, say, especially after 35, and everyone's age was at the same time, and I don't think Whiteman would have had a chance to have T. Garden or Biderbecke or any of these guys. They would have more likely have been with bands that were swinging more, playing more, you see. But in those days, this kind of hotel band was the dominant band, and there weren't as many of them. Radio multiplied them. Once radio really took hold, it multiplied them radio and records. But in the early 1920s, the really big names, you could pretty well know most of them. In the 30s you couldn't. It would take you all day to recite the number of bands there were. You just wouldn't remember all of them.
So what you had then was a lot of bands with local reputations, territory bands I guess they called them.

Oh, far from territory. You mean generally? Before the 30s. Well, the bands I mentioned, like Lopez and Whiteman, of course, were nationally known. Yeah. They were the, Saratoga got the best that could be gotten. It was very wealthy. And it's one month, actually for one month, the month of August, when the racing season was on. Maybe a five week season or so. Sometimes it was. But there were territory bands, of course. New England was loaded with a number of them. And the New York. Western New York, Pennsylvania, and Jersey area was loaded with a number of them. Some of them were bands that later became big name bands in the 30s. They were embryonic. They were on their way. Sometimes there were bands put together for summer barnstorming, college kids and the like. And a lot of them went on to… I remember one band that came in from New England named Don Gann. If I remember correctly, Gann or Gann. Most of which later became the Les Brown band. The early Les Brown band.
Yet he came out of Duke, didn't he?
I know it. I've never reconciled that. But somebody that really dug into newspapers in those days, or whatever other sources there were, could maybe unravel things like that.
Well, those personnel were subject to change, I'm very reckoning.

Yes, and whether Les Brown had joined this Don Gann band, or whether he just took it over, or whether he may have been an arranger for it. Quite often the kind of story that you heard about how a band originated was romanticized, you know. And it'd give you the impression that this band had stuck together and fought its way up writers and movies and things like to depict things that way. That was hardly ever true. Very seldom did it happen. Usually as the band moved up, the personnel changed. Got better.
Well yeah, and Alito, his band broke up, he might just take up another man's band entirely.
Or higher, and anyway, temperaments being what they were, very few musicians could stand anybody very long in there. Always splitting up, moving up, moving around.
